p: Four years ago, in October eighteen seventy-one, Mr Charles Babbage died in his house in Dorset Street, London, a disappointed and quarrelsome old man, at war with the organ-grinders of the neighbourhood, whose music he could not abide, and with most of the scientific establishment of the kingdom. He left behind him drawers full of plans for machines that had never been built. I met him once, at one of his famous Saturday evening parties, where he displayed a small working fragment of his first machine, and a silver lady, an automaton that danced. I was more impressed by the lady. I now understand that I was a fool.

Babbage's first design, which he called the Difference Engine, was a machine of brass gearwheels for calculating mathematical tables, of the kind used by navigators and actuaries, without the errors that human calculators, then called computers, inevitably made. The government gave him seventeen thousand pounds, an enormous sum, and after twenty years, a quarrel with his engineer and many changes of plan, abandoned the project. By then he had conceived something far more ambitious, an Analytical Engine, which would not merely calculate tables but could be instructed, by cards punched with holes, like those that control the patterns woven by the Jacquard looms of Lyon, to carry out any sequence of calculations whatever. It would have a store, in which numbers were held, and a mill, in which they were operated upon, and it could decide what to do next according to the results of its own calculations. It was never built.

Its most perceptive interpreter was Augusta Ada, Countess of Lovelace, the daughter of Lord Byron, who in eighteen forty-three translated an Italian account of the engine and added notes three times as long as the original. In them she described how the engine might be instructed to calculate a certain series of numbers, which is often called the first computer program, and observed something Babbage himself had not stressed: that the engine might act upon other things besides numbers, if their relations could be expressed in symbols, and that it might, for instance, compose elaborate pieces of music. She added, however, that the engine has no pretensions to originate anything; it can do only whatever we know how to order it to perform. Remember that sentence. We shall meet it again. She died in eighteen fifty-two, at thirty-six, the same age as her father.

The Encyclopaedia tells me that Babbage's dream was realised, in a quite different form, in the twentieth century, and that the man who first understood its full meaning was a young English mathematician named Alan Turing, born in London in nineteen twelve. In nineteen thirty-six, at the age of twenty-four, a Fellow of King's College, Cambridge, he published a paper on a question in the foundations of mathematics, whether there could be a mechanical method for deciding the truth of any mathematical statement. To answer it, he imagined a machine of the simplest possible kind: an endless tape of paper divided into squares, a head that can read and write a symbol on one square at a time and move the tape one square left or right, and a short table of rules telling it what to do next, depending on what it reads and on its present state. He showed, to the astonishment of the mathematicians, that such a machine, simple as it is, could carry out any calculation that can be done by any set of mechanical rules whatever; and that one such machine, given the rules of another written upon its tape, could imitate any other. This is what the men of the future call a universal machine. Every calculating machine of the future, from the greatest to the one in a child's pocket, is in principle such a machine. He also proved that there are questions that no such machine can ever answer, which is a comfort to some of us.

In the Second World War, Turing worked at a secret establishment at Bletchley Park, in Buckinghamshire, where mathematicians, linguists, chess players and many hundreds of young women laboured to read the coded messages of the German armed forces. The Germans used a machine called Enigma, a typewriter with rotating wheels that scrambled each letter differently at every keystroke, which they believed unbreakable. Building on the earlier work of Polish mathematicians, Turing designed electrical machines called bombes that searched rapidly through the possible settings of the Enigma, and the intelligence obtained, among other things, helped to defeat the German submarines that were starving Britain. His colleagues at Bletchley built, for another German cipher, an electronic calculating machine called Colossus, one of the first in the world. It was kept secret for thirty years.

After the war, Turing designed one of the first electronic computers with a stored program and worked on another at Manchester. In nineteen fifty he published a paper asking, can machines think? He proposed to replace the question with a test: if a machine, conversing by written messages, could not be distinguished by a judge from a human being, we should have no better reason to deny it thought than we have to deny it to one another. He discussed Lady Lovelace's objection directly, and doubted it.

His end was shameful, not to him but to my country. In nineteen fifty-two, he was prosecuted for a private relationship with another man, which was then a crime, and, to avoid prison, submitted to a course of chemical treatment. He was found dead in June nineteen fifty-four, poisoned by cyanide, at the age of forty-one; the inquest found that he had killed himself, though some have doubted it. In two thousand and nine, the Encyclopaedia records, the British Prime Minister apologised for his treatment, and in two thousand and thirteen the Queen pardoned him. His face now appears on the fifty-pound note of the Bank of England, which I suspect would have amused him.

The first electronic computers, built in America and Britain in the nineteen-forties, filled large rooms with thousands of glowing glass valves, consumed great quantities of electricity, and broke down frequently. Then, in nineteen forty-seven, three physicists at the Bell Telephone Laboratories, a company descended from Mr Bell's, invented the transistor, a tiny switch made from crystals, and from the late nineteen-fifties engineers learned to make many such switches together on a single small chip of a substance called silicon. The number that could be placed on one chip doubled roughly every two years, for half a century and more, until a chip the size of a fingernail held many billions. The calculating power that once filled a room came to sit on a desk, and then in a pocket.

I have spent much of my life with ledgers and tables and indexes, and I have some idea what these machines would have meant to me. I think of Babbage, scowling at the organ-grinders, and of Lady Lovelace, writing her notes in a house in St James's Square, and of Turing, running across country, as I learn he did, at the pace of an Olympic athlete. Between them they changed what it means to think. And the story is not finished.
